title: SN1 and E1 products: racemization and the shared carbocation
asks: A substrate ionizes in a polar protic solvent. Draw the substitution and elimination products and their stereochemistry.

know.h: The conditions. {{SN1}} and {{E1}} need four things: a substrate that gives a stable carbocation, a good leaving group, a polar protic solvent (water or an alcohol), and a poor nucleophile that is also a weak base. In practice the solvent is the only nucleophile and the only base in the flask.

Which carbons ionize. Tertiary ionizes fastest, then secondary. Primary and methyl never do: no {{SN1}}, no {{E1}}. Allylic and benzylic carbons do ionize, even when they are primary or secondary, because the neighbouring pi electrons share the charge. A vinyl carbon (the leaving group on a C=C carbon) never ionizes.
The rate law. rate = k[substrate]. The slow step is the ionization of the substrate alone, so adding more nucleophile changes nothing.

{{SN1}} with water or an alcohol is three steps. (1) The leaving group leaves and a carbocation forms. (2) A lone pair on the oxygen of the solvent attacks the positive carbon. (3) A second solvent molecule removes the extra proton from the positive oxygen. Be able to draw all three with arrows.
What the product is. In water the substitution product is an alcohol, R-OH. In an alcohol R'OH it is an ether, R-OR'. The new oxygen group comes from the solvent, so read the solvent before you draw.

Racemization. The carbocation is flat ({{sp2}}, three groups in one plane). The nucleophile can approach from either face, so one enantiomer of starting material gives both enantiomers of product in equal amounts: a racemic mixture. The lecture example is 2-butyl tosylate in water.
A second stereocentre changes the word. If the molecule has another stereocentre that is not touched, attack on the two faces gives two diastereomers, not a racemic mixture.

{{E1}} shares the carbocation. Instead of attacking the positive carbon, a solvent molecule takes a hydrogen from the carbon next to it, and the C-H electrons become the C=C. {{E1}} is two steps, and its first step is the same as in {{SN1}}.
Temperature decides the ratio. {{SN1}} is favoured at lower temperature and {{E1}} at high temperature. Both products usually form together.

Which alkene. Every different carbon next to the positive carbon that has a hydrogen gives an alkene. The more substituted alkene (Saytzeff, also spelled Zaitsev) is the major elimination product. The double bond always includes the carbon that carried the leaving group.
Leaving groups. {{I-}}, {{Br-}}, {{Cl-}} and tosylate ({{TsO-}}) are good leaving groups. {{HO-}} and {{F-}} are not, so an alcohol or a fluoride does not ionize under these conditions.

An allylic cation has two positive ends. Its charge is shared by the two end carbons of the three-carbon unit. The nucleophile can bond to either end, so two substitution products can form, one of them with the double bond moved.

Carbocations can rearrange. Before you finish, check whether a neighbouring hydrogen or carbon group could move to give a more stable cation. That question has its own page: carbocation rearrangements.
Skill. Be able to draw the carbocation (three bonds, a plus sign, no wedges), and both enantiomers of the product with a wedge and a dash.

method: Classify the carbon that carries the leaving group. Tertiary, secondary, allylic and benzylic can ionize. Primary, methyl and vinyl cannot.

Read the conditions. A polar protic solvent with no strong base and no good nucleophile means the carbocation route. If a strong base such as {{HO-}} or {{RO-}} is present, stop: that is {{E2}}, not this page.
Remove the leaving group with its electrons and draw the carbocation, flat, with its plus sign.
Ask whether the charge is anywhere else: resonance in an allylic or benzylic cation, or a shift to a more stable cation.
Substitution: bond the solvent's oxygen to the positive carbon, then take the extra hydrogen off the oxygen. If that carbon is a stereocentre, draw both faces.
Elimination: take a hydrogen from each different neighbouring carbon in turn and draw each alkene. Mark the most substituted one as major.
Say which product the conditions favour: heat favours the alkene, a lower temperature favours substitution.

pitfalls.h: Drawing only the inverted product. Inversion belongs to {{SN2}}. {{SN1}} at a stereocentre gives both enantiomers.
Stopping after the solvent attacks, with the hydrogen and a positive charge still on oxygen. The third step, loss of the proton, is part of the mechanism and the product is neutral.
Using {{HO-}} or {{RO-}} as the nucleophile or the base. In water or an alcohol with nothing added, only the neutral solvent is there.
Ionizing a primary, methyl or vinyl carbon. Those carbocations do not form.
Writing "racemic" when the molecule keeps another stereocentre. The two products are then diastereomers.
Putting the double bond between two carbons that do not include the carbon the leaving group left.
